title: The Marriage to Khadijah
teaser: She had refused the nobles of Quraysh. Then she sent a friend to ask a man who worked for her.

layers.title: The Setting
layers.subtitle: A woman with capital, a man with none
layers.content:
Makkah produced almost nothing. It ate what came up the road from Yemen and it lived off what went down the road to Syria, and the men of Quraysh were merchants before they were anything else. Standing in that city was measured in caravans financed, goods delivered, debts honoured.

He had no trade of his own. Al-Mubarakpuri records only that he was reported to have herded sheep for Bani Sa'd, and in Makkah for a wage, and Sahih al-Bukhari carries the shepherding as ordinary prophetic work rather than as anything remarkable. At twenty-five he had a name in the market and no capital to put behind it.

Khadijah bint Khuwailid had both. Ibn Sa'd traces her line — Khuwailid ibn Asad ibn Abd al-Uzza ibn Qusayy — into the old stock of Quraysh. Ibn Ishaq, quoted by al-Mubarakpuri, calls her a businesswoman of great honour and fortune who used to employ men to trade on her behalf for an agreed share of the profits. She did not walk the routes herself. She funded them and chose who walked them, which in a merchant town is the harder skill.

She was already being asked for. Many prominent men of Quraysh had sought her hand and she had turned every one of them down. That is the position she was in when she was told about him — not weighing a suitor, but hearing a name in her own trade attached to truthful speech, plain honesty and good manners.

So she sent for him.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Hiring — the shepherding of the prophets
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam; Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kubra, Vol. III

layers.title: What Happened
layers.subtitle: A commercial offer, then a proposal sent sideways
layers.content:
The offer she made him was commercial and it was generous. She would pay him at a higher rate than she paid her other agents to carry her goods north to Syria, and she would send her own servant, Maisarah, along with him. He agreed, and the two of them went.

The northern road was weeks of travelling, up the length of the Hijaz and out of Arabia altogether. What the sirah keeps is not the journey but its accounting. When he came back, al-Mubarakpuri writes, Khadijah found greater profit and greater blessing in that consignment than she was used to. And Maisarah, who had watched him at close quarters for the whole distance, reported on the man and not on the margin — his manners, his honesty, the depth of his thought, his sincerity.

It was on that double report, the ledger and the servant, that she formed the wish to marry him. She did not put it to him herself. She disclosed it to her friend Nafisah, daughter of Muniyah, and Nafisah went to him immediately and told him.

He agreed, and then did it the formal way. He asked his uncles to go and speak to Khadijah's uncle. The matter was settled, and the marriage agreement was witnessed by Banu Hashim and by the chiefs of Mudar. He gave twenty camels as her dowry.

She was forty years old. He was twenty-five. Al-Mubarakpuri, following the sirah, calls her the best of women in lineage, fortune and wisdom. She was the first woman he married, and while she lived he married no one else.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam, citing Ibn Hisham 1/187-188

layers.title: The Turning Point
layers.subtitle: What the marriage quietly put in one house
layers.content:
Look at what this one marriage put under a single roof, because almost everyone in it matters later.

Zayd bin Harithah arrived first. Ibn Sa'd gives the whole route. A boy visiting his mother's people among the Banu Ma'n of Tayy, carried off by raiders of Banu al-Qayn, taken to the market at Ukaz and offered for sale there, bought for four hundred dirhams by Hakim bin Hizam for his aunt Khadijah. When she married, she gave the boy to her husband, and he took him. Ibn Sa'd also records that when the early scholars disagreed over who the first Muslim was, the three names they argued between were Abu Bakr, Ali, and Zayd bin Harithah — the boy from this household.

Then the children. Al-Mubarakpuri names them: al-Qasim, Zainab, Ruqaiyah, Umm Kulthum, Fatimah, and Abdullah, who is also called Tayyib and Tahir. Every son died in childhood. Every daughter except Fatimah died in his lifetime, and Fatimah outlived him by six months. All four daughters lived to see Islam, accepted it, and made the journey to Madinah.

The hinge of the chapter is one sentence in Ibn Sa'd. The early authorities, he reports, agreed that the first of the people of the qibla to respond to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was Khadijah bint Khuwailid. Fifteen years of watching how a man handled her money, her agents and her word came before that. When the claim finally came to her, she was not talked into believing it. She had already formed her assessment of him, in conditions where dishonesty would have shown, and the assessment held.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kubra, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley; Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar

layers.title: The Revelation
layers.subtitle: No ayah for this marriage, only a principle
layers.content:
No revelation came down about this marriage. It happened some fifteen years before the cave, and the Qur'an does not narrate it. That should be said plainly, because a chapter set this early stands before the text and has to be read on the testimony of the sirah alone.

What the Qur'an offers instead is the principle the marriage answers to: «وَمِنْ آيَاتِهِ أَنْ خَلَقَ لَكُم مِّنْ أَنفُسِكُمْ أَزْوَاجًا لِّتَسْكُنُوا إِلَيْهَا وَجَعَلَ بَيْنَكُم مَّوَدَّةً وَرَحْمَةً» — 'And of His signs is that He created for you, from yourselves, mates, that you may find rest in them; and He placed between you affection and mercy.' (30:21) The ayah names rest first, before anything else it might have named.

What the hadith offers is his own verdict on her, given years after she was dead. Musnad Ahmad preserves it: she believed in him when the people disbelieved him, she trusted him when the people called him a liar, she helped and comforted him with her person and her wealth when the people would not, and Allah gave him children by her.

And Sahih al-Bukhari carries the greeting. Abu Hurayrah narrated that Jibreel came to the Prophet ﷺ and told him Khadijah was on her way with a vessel of food or drink, and that when she came he should give her greetings from her Lord and glad tidings of a house in Paradise in which there is no noise and no toil.

A greeting sent down for one woman, by name, carried by the angel of revelation. Nothing in the sirah is said about a marriage more strongly than that.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 30:21 — «وَمِنْ آيَاتِهِ أَنْ خَلَقَ لَكُم مِّنْ أَنفُسِكُمْ أَزْوَاجًا لِّتَسْكُنُوا إِلَيْهَا» 'And of His signs is that He created for you, from yourselves, mates, that you may find rest in them'
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Hurayrah — Jibreel's greeting to Khadijah; and Musnad Ahmad — 'She believed in me while the people disbelieved in me'
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam, citing Musnad Ahmad 6/118 and Sahih Al-Bukhari 1/539

layers.title: What It Left Behind
layers.subtitle: Twenty-five years, and the thing worth carrying
layers.content:
Twenty-five years and one wife, in a society that placed no limit on the number. Al-Mubarakpuri states it without decoration: she was the only wife he had until she died, and it was only after her death — a loss that belongs to a later chapter — that he married again. Whatever else can be argued about the households of Arabia, this arrangement was chosen under no obligation and kept for a quarter of a century.

The house also drew the family lines of the community that came afterwards. Zainab was married before the Hijra to her cousin Abul-As bin ar-Rabi'. Ruqaiyah and Umm Kulthum were married in turn to Uthman bin Affan, the second after the death of the first. Fatimah was married to Ali bin Abi Talib in the period between Badr and Uhud, and her sons were al-Hasan and al-Husain. A surprising amount of the first century of Islam runs back through one Makkan house.

But the thing to carry out of this chapter is smaller and harder than any of that.

At twenty-five he had no capital, no trade of his own, no standing beyond his clan, and no message. What he had was a reputation for honesty that other people had formed by watching him work — in transactions where a small lie would have paid, and where the only witness was a servant. That reputation is what produced the offer, the journey, the marriage, and, fifteen years later, the first person on earth to believe him.

Nobody argued her into faith. She had audited him for years without knowing that was what she was doing. Character is being assessed continuously, by people who will never tell you they are assessing it, and the verdict arrives at the moment it matters most.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam — The Prophetic Household

quiz.prompt: What arrangement did Khadijah offer him before there was any question of marriage?

options.text: A loan so that he could finance his own caravan
A higher rate than her other agents to carry her goods to Syria, with her servant Maisarah accompanying him
A share in her household in exchange for managing her flocks
A permanent position as scribe over her accounts in Makkah

quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, citing Ibn Ishaq
quiz.scholar_reflection: She employed men on a percentage of the profit. He was offered more than the others before anyone had met him — his reputation was already priced into the deal.

quiz.prompt: Who carried Khadijah's wish for marriage to him?

options.text: Her uncle, who negotiated directly with Abu Talib
Maisarah, the servant who had travelled with him
Her friend Nafisah, daughter of Muniyah
She sent no one and spoke to him herself

quiz.scholar_reflection: Nafisah went to him at once. He agreed, and then asked his uncles to approach Khadijah's uncle so that the matter would be settled in the proper form.

quiz.prompt: What did he give Khadijah as her dowry?

options.text: Twenty camels
Four hundred dirhams
A house in the upper quarter of Makkah
One hundred camels and two horses

quiz.scholar_reflection: Twenty camels, witnessed by Banu Hashim and the chiefs of Mudar. Four hundred dirhams is the price Ibn Sa'd gives for something else in this chapter — the purchase of Zayd bin Harithah at the market of Ukaz.

quiz.prompt: According to Ibn Sa'd, whom did the early authorities agree was the first of the people of the qibla to respond to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ?

options.text: Abu Bakr as-Siddiq
Khadijah bint Khuwailid
Ali bin Abi Talib
Zayd bin Harithah

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kubra, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Ibn Sa'd reports agreement on Khadijah, and disagreement only about who came after her — Abu Bakr, Ali, or Zayd bin Harithah.

quiz.prompt: In the narration of Abu Hurayrah in Sahih al-Bukhari, what did Jibreel tell the Prophet ﷺ to convey to Khadijah?

options.text: That her wealth would be returned to her manyfold in this world
That she would live to see Makkah accept the message
Greetings from her Lord, and glad tidings of a house in Paradise in which there is no noise and no toil
That her name would be recited in the Qur'an

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Hurayrah — reported in Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: She was coming to him with a vessel of food or drink at the time. The greeting was sent down while she was mid-errand, doing something ordinary.

quiz.prompt: She was forty, wealthy, and had refused the leading men of Quraysh. She then chose a man of twenty-five with a reputation and no capital. What do you think she was actually assessing?

options.text: Character, which she could verify herself, over wealth, which she already had
Risk — she ran a business, and needed a man she could not be defrauded by
Something she perceived that the sources do not record, and that we should not invent
All three at once — the sirah gives us the decision and leaves us the motives

quiz.slider_label: How much weight do you give character over circumstance?
quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the account of the proposal
quiz.scholar_reflection: The sources tell us what she had been told about him: truthful words, honesty, good manners. They do not tell us what she felt. It is better to leave that gap open than to fill it.

quiz.prompt: Maisarah came back and reported on his manners rather than on the profit. Whose testimony about you would carry that kind of weight?

options.text: A servant on the road had nothing to gain by flattering him — the report is credible because of who gave it
The people who work beside you see the version of you that actually exists
He was the same man in Busra as he was in Makkah, with no audience that could reward him
All of these — the identity of the witness is the whole force of the story

quiz.slider_label: How consistent are you when nobody who matters is watching?
quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — Maisarah's report to Khadijah
quiz.scholar_reflection: A hired man's word about his employer's agent is not the kind of evidence anyone stages. That is precisely why the sirah keeps it.

quiz.prompt: No revelation came down about this marriage. How do you read a chapter of a prophet's life on which the Qur'an is silent?

options.text: Silence is not absence — the Qur'an gives the principle instead, and 30:21 is that principle
It is a reminder that most of a life is not scripture, and still counts for something
Here the sirah does the work, and the sirah is human testimony with its own disagreements
All of these — the silence is itself instructive about what revelation is for

quiz.slider_label: How comfortable are you with parts of the story scripture does not narrate?
quiz.citation: Quran 30:21 — the ayah of mates, affection and mercy
quiz.scholar_reflection: Fifteen years of his life pass in this chapter with no ayah attached to them. What the Qur'an did eventually send down about her was a greeting, not a narrative.

quiz.prompt: Every son born in that house died in childhood, and three of the four daughters died in his lifetime. Most of that grief came before any of the public events. What does knowing it change?

options.text: It places the losses before the mission rather than as a price paid for it
It means the patience he later taught was something he had already been charged for
It is a caution against reading divine favour as exemption from ordinary sorrow
All of these — the household is a quieter argument than any battle

quiz.slider_label: How do you hold grief and purpose in the same hand?
quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — The Prophetic Household
quiz.scholar_reflection: Al-Qasim and Abdullah. Zainab, Ruqaiyah, Umm Kulthum. He buried nearly all of his children. Fatimah alone outlived him, by six months.

quiz.prompt: Twenty-five years with one wife, in a society that imposed no limit. What do you take from a choice made under no obligation at all?

options.text: Choices made freely reveal more than choices made under a rule
This was not a law being obeyed — it was a relationship being kept
A standard set by conduct lands harder than a standard set by instruction
All of these — and none of it was legislated for anyone else

quiz.slider_label: Which do you trust more in yourself — the rule or the habit?
quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — 'She was the first woman he married; he did not marry any other until she passed away'
quiz.scholar_reflection: There was no verse requiring it and no custom expecting it. It was simply what he did for a quarter of a century, and the record notes it as a fact rather than as a virtue.
